doc.title: Mona Hinton interviewed by Milt Fillius and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Clockers soundtrack and Quincy Jones's torn check tribute
summary: Milt first recorded in 1930 and recently played on Spike Lee's Clockers; Quincy Jones's birthday video shows the check Milt tore up after Quincy's first date as leader.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Spike. He just did the soundtrack for Spike’s new movie called “Clockers” I think is the name of it. So since 1930, he has worked with every musician. And I must tell you an interesting story about Quincy. For Milton’s 80th birthday I think it was, he sent a home made video, a homemade videotape to the house, and he had someone take it. And he’s standing there with his envelope and piece of paper, and he says, “Bring the camera up I want you to be sure and see this, that Milt can see that this is his handwriting and this is his torn check.” And he tells a story on this tape saying that on his first recording date that any company allowed him to do under his own name, I don’t know whether the copyist messed up or whatever but anyway the date had to go into overtime. The company held him responsible for the overtime, and here is a young kid, his first recording date under his own name, didn’t have a dime. And so anyway, he borrowed and stole and got ahold of the money, and he paid every musician the money that was due them. And he says you know every musician took that money except you, Milton, and here’s, he reads the letter and he shows Milton the letter that Milton returned to him, and Milton evidently had torn the check and put it in the letter. And he says, “and here’s his torn check.” He said, “I have had this all these years in the front of my datebook,” and he said, “every day that God allows me to get up, I look at this and keep reminding me of what some of my responsibilities are to other young people.” Now I think that’s a great tribute. But that’s really basically the way Milton has always lived. I mean he’s always trying to help, you know, promote the young people and encourage them or whatnot, and I think that’s the best example of what I’m saying. And I think it’s a great honor that he would keep that all these years, and that was one part of his birthday present to Milton, I think on his 80th birthday but I’m not sure.
I think there’s a tremendous message in that —
For musicians, young musicians today, who are hungry for the trappings without affording each other the camaraderie and support. That’s what the music is really about. Am I right?
